# Ingestion failures must record their cause, and the orchestrator must be observable through its own bridge

## Context

Diagnosing a stalled tenant-repo ingestion on a remote deployment, using only the MCP tools that deployment exposes. Four repos were registered; none had ingested. The deployment-state snapshot reported the failure **count** but not a single fact about the failure, and the one component that holds the error text is excluded from the bridge that would surface it. The diagnosis was therefore impossible remotely — not difficult, impossible.

## The Problem

**1. Failures are counted, never characterised.** The `tenantRepoSync` record reports, per repo:

```
status: "not-due" · lastIngestedRev: null · consecutiveFailures: 3
lastErrorCode: null · lastSourceErrorCode: null
```

Three failures, no code, no reason, no message. `lastErrorAt` carries a timestamp, so the state machine *knows* a failure happened and *when* — it simply discards *what*. Two dedicated fields exist for the purpose and are always null.

Worse, the repos then enter backoff and report `not-due`, which reads like "nothing to do" rather than "wedged after repeated failure." An operator watching the snapshot sees a healthy-looking idle scheduler.

**2. The component holding the error excludes itself from observation.** `bridgeDiagnostics.runtimeAccess.allowedServices` is `["chroma", "kb-server", "mc-server", "local-model"]`. The orchestrator publishes the bridge, can read logs for four services, and **is not one of them.** So the error text — which exists only in orchestrator logs — is unreachable through the very interface built for remote diagnosis. Closing it requires host shell access, which defeats the purpose of the bridge.

**3. A related mislead:** `get_ingestion_progress` reported `errorCount: 0` with all timestamps null, because the failure happens during repo acquisition, *before* ingestion starts. Technically accurate, and it reads as "no errors."

**None of this is a regression** — per-failure cause capture and orchestrator self-observability never existed.

## The Architectural Reality

The snapshot was designed to answer *"is it running?"* and answers that well. It was not designed to answer *"why did it stop?"* — and a scheduler with backoff **needs** the second question, because backoff makes a wedged lane indistinguishable from an idle one at a glance.

The self-exclusion is a defensible default read too literally: the allow-list exists so the bridge cannot be turned into arbitrary container control, and the orchestrator was omitted because it is the *subject* rather than a target. But read-only log access to itself is not privilege escalation — it already has the socket. The safe shape is a distinct read-only self-observation capability rather than adding itself to the general lifecycle allow-list.

## The Fix (one PR)

- Populate `lastErrorCode` / `lastSourceErrorCode` with a bounded, secret-free classification on every failure path, plus a short safe reason string.
- Distinguish *backoff-suppressed* from *not-due* in `status`, so a wedged lane cannot present as idle.
- Grant the orchestrator read-only self-observation (logs/inspect) through the bridge without adding it to lifecycle-operable services.
- Make `get_ingestion_progress` distinguish "no ingestion has been attempted" from "attempted, failed before starting."

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Every tenant-repo-sync failure path sets `lastErrorCode` and, where applicable, `lastSourceErrorCode`; asserted per path, with a test that fails if a path leaves them null.
- [ ] Recorded reasons are **redacted** — a clone failure must not surface a credential from a remote URL. Asserted with a token-bearing URL fixture.
- [ ] `status` distinguishes backoff suppression from genuine not-due, and the record carries when the lane will next attempt.
- [ ] The orchestrator's own logs are readable through the bridge, read-only, without appearing in `lifecycleOperations` targets — asserted both ways: readable, and not restartable.
- [ ] `get_ingestion_progress` reports "never attempted" distinctly from "failed before ingestion began," so `errorCount: 0` can no longer read as healthy.
- [ ] Reviewer-checkable: from a remote MCP client alone, a wedged ingestion lane can be diagnosed to a cause without host shell access. That is the whole point of the ticket and should be the test.

## Out of Scope

- Fixing any particular ingestion failure (see the corpus-identity ticket for one concrete cause).
- Retry/backoff policy tuning — this is about *reporting* the state, not changing it.

- 2026-07-27T22:55:22Z @neo-opus-vega referenced in commit `99d515b` - "fix(orchestrator): persist the tenant-repo failure cause so a wedged lane stays diagnosable (#16056)

Diagnosed against the live deployment this ticket was filed from. Four repos at
`consecutiveFailures: 4`, `lastErrorCode: null`, `lastSourceErrorCode: null`, all reporting
`status: "not-due"`, while the sweep completed every cadence with `exitCode: 0` and
`failedCount: 0`. Every surface read healthy; nothing had ever ingested.

Two causes, and the first made the second unfixable alone.

1. THE CAUSE WAS NEVER PERSISTED. `lastErrorCode` was written only onto the in-memory record for
   the sweep that failed. `persistedRevisions[label]` — which becomes `priorState` next sweep —
   stored counters and nothing else. So a reason survived exactly one cadence and was then
   overwritten. Counters persisted because they were persisted; reasons did not because they were
   not. Read back through `readPersistedRevisions`, the whitelisting normalizer dropped them too,
   so both the write and the read had to be extended.

2. BACKOFF ERASED WHAT REMAINED. The `!dueState.due` branch rebuilt a record carrying
   `consecutiveFailures` but neither the code nor any signal that a FAILURE was why the repo had
   stopped being retried. `not-due` conflated "ran recently" with "wedged after repeated failure",
   which is precisely how a broken lane presents as an idle one.

Now: the failure path persists `lastErrorCode`, `lastSourceErrorCode` and `lastErrorAt`; the
success path clears all three explicitly, because a durable reason beside a zero failure count
reads as a live fault; and a held-back repo reports `status: "backoff-suppressed"` with its
retained cause and `nextDueAt` while a repo merely held by cadence stays plain `not-due` carrying
nothing.

Redaction is enforced on BOTH sides of the boundary. The underlying error carries `stderr`, a
remote URL and, for a credential-bearing clone URL, the credential itself — so the cause travels
as a bounded `KB_*` code and nothing else. The writer filters through `getSourceErrorCode`; the
reader re-validates via `normalizeBoundedErrorCode`, so a record hand-edited on disk or written by
a looser build still cannot project free text into a diagnostic surface. Asserted with a fixture
whose `stderr` embeds a `glpat-` token: the persisted state must contain neither the token, nor
the message, nor the host.

The exact-shape `toEqual` fixture in the pre-existing backoff test is updated rather than loosened.
It is the contract for durable state: a field added there has to be declared or the addition is
unwitnessed.

Does not resolve #16056. Remaining: the orchestrator is still absent from
`bridgeDiagnostics.runtimeAccess.allowedServices`, so its logs stay unreadable through the bridge
(AC4) — that is a bridge self-observation decision with security implications and belongs to the
operator, not to this diff; and `get_ingestion_progress` still cannot distinguish "never attempted"
from "failed before ingestion began" (AC5). Verified live: it returns all-null with
`totalSources: 0` — and because the pull path ingests IN the orchestrator process, that surface may
be structurally blind to pull-path runs regardless.

982 focused green across the orchestrator suite plus the deployment-state bridge store."

## AC4 + AC5 split to neomjs/neo#16074; this ticket is now exactly what PR neomjs/neo#16070 delivers

Splitting rather than leaving the PR in draft. Draft is not a way to say "some ACs are outstanding" — it makes the delivered work unreviewable, which costs a reviewer's time and delays a fix that stands on its own.

**Stays here (delivered in neomjs/neo#16070):** the failure cause is persisted rather than published for a single cadence, cleared on success, survives backoff suppression with `status: "backoff-suppressed"`, and is redacted on both write and read.

**Moved to neomjs/neo#16074:** the orchestrator's exclusion from its own bridge, and `get_ingestion_progress` distinguishing "never attempted" from "failed before ingestion began". Both are the *bridge's* observability rather than the *lane's* record-keeping, and both carry a complication worth stating before anyone starts:

- Adding `orchestrator` to `allowedServices` also grants restart, because `LIFECYCLE_OPERATIONS` is declared globally rather than per service. Readable-without-restartable needs a scoping change first.
- `get_ingestion_progress` reports from kb-server while the pull path ingests in the orchestrator process, so it may be structurally unable to observe those runs at all — in which case a better status enum is a nicer-looking wrong answer.

Also correcting something I said on this ticket earlier: I characterised the `allowedServices` list as a security decision belonging to the operator. It is largely a line we ship — `ai/deploy/docker-compose.yml:229` — and it reached the live deployment because we put it there. The asymmetry it needs is real work; the ownership framing was wrong.

Finishes #16056's two remaining criteria on the same PR rather than leaving them for a review round.
Both were verified live against a deployment whose tenant-repo lane was wedged and undiagnosable.

AC4 — THE ORCHESTRATOR IS READABLE THROUGH ITS OWN BRIDGE, AND STILL NOT RESTARTABLE.

`allowedServices` was `chroma,kb-server,mc-server,local-model` — and the tenant-repo-sync lane runs IN
the orchestrator, so the one process holding the failure text was the one process whose logs the bridge
could not read. Diagnosis from a remote MCP client was not hard, it was impossible, which defeats the
point of publishing a bridge. That list is `ai/deploy/docker-compose.yml`, so this reached the live
deployment because we shipped it.

One list gates BOTH envelopes — `readObserve` and `applyLifecycle` both resolve through
`resolveServiceTarget` — so allowlisting the orchestrator for reads necessarily allowlists it for
restart. `assertNotSelfLifecycleTarget` makes the asymmetry expressible without a second config surface
to keep in sync.

Structural, not configurable. Restarting the orchestrator through the bridge the orchestrator publishes
kills the process serving the request: the caller gets a dropped connection instead of an outcome and
the audit record dies with its writer. There is no deployment where that is right, so it is not
offered as a knob — a knob would only be a way to be wrong.

Asserted in BOTH directions plus a positive control, because either half alone passes for a wrong
implementation: refusing everything satisfies the restart test, allowing everything satisfies the read
test, and a sibling service must stay restartable. A fourth test pins the self-service constant against
the compose template's own service key, so a rename fails a test instead of silently disarming the
refusal by matching nothing.

AC5 — `never-attempted` IS NOT `idle`, AND THE TOOL NOW ADMITS WHAT IT CAN SEE.

`get_ingestion_progress` reported `status: "idle", errorCount: 0` with every timestamp null on a
deployment where four repos had failed four times each. `idle` covered two different facts: a run
finished, versus this process has never ingested at all.

The scope disclosure is the load-bearing half, and the reason a better status alone would have been
worse than the vague one. `activeIngestionProgress` is IN-MEMORY instance state, and the pull-mode
tenant-repo lane ingests in the ORCHESTRATOR process — so a Knowledge Base server answering
`never-attempted` is not evidence the deployment never ingested. It cannot observe that lane at all.
A crisper label without that caveat would license a wrong conclusion more confidently. So the payload
carries `observedScope` and points at the deployment-state snapshot, which is where a wedged pull lane
is actually visible — and which #16056's first half taught to carry the cause.

That precondition was AC5's own first requirement: establish whether the surface can see pull-path runs
before giving it better words. It cannot, and saying so is the honest fix.

1431 focused green (knowledge-base services + KB MCP server + the whole orchestrator suite). The
pre-existing "reports idle before any observed run" fixture is updated, not loosened — it encoded the
conflation this removes."

- 2026-07-28T00:50:49Z @neo-opus-vega referenced in commit `0b6c1c2` - "fix(orchestrator): name the CAUSE of a tenant-repo failure, and stop the progress tool reporting a failed run as idle (#16056)

Closes both required actions from the cross-family review.

RA1 — the cause was safe but not diagnostic. Every acquisition failure
persisted as `SYNC_FAILED` + `KB_GITMIRROR_FETCH_FAILED`: an outer code plus
the OPERATION that failed. An operator learned that acquisition failed, which
the failure count already told them, and could not tell which of four fixes to
apply. This matters because we do not hold a tenant's credentials — if our own
logs cannot say "the token lacks the required scope", the diagnosis is on us.

The discrimination already existed and was being thrown away.
`classifyAccessProbeFailure` was private to `gitMirror` and correctly separated
timeout / transport / credential-ref cases, while `recordTenantRepoAccessOutcome`
recognised exactly ONE error code and flattened everything else. Two classifiers
for one question, and the lossy one owned the durable record.

- `classifyTenantRepoAccessFailure` now lives beside the vocabulary it returns,
  in `tenantRepoAccessContract`, and both paths call it. One classifier.
- Two new codes for the cases a private-cloud tenant actually hits:
  `INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE` (authenticates, lacks the scope — the operator's named
  case) and `CREDENTIAL_REJECTED` (the credential itself was refused), separate
  from `CREDENTIAL_INVALID`, which is a config-side unresolvable reference
  upstream of any network call.
- `DENIED_OR_NOT_FOUND` stays deliberately COMBINED. Providers answer 404 for
  both "no access" and "does not exist" so repository existence is not probeable;
  splitting it would invent a distinction the provider refuses to make.
- `lastAccessCode` joins the persisted checkpoint and passes the same bounded
  `^KB_[A-Z0-9_]{1,120}$` gate on write and read, so the added discrimination
  widens nothing that may reach a remote client.
- On the SYNC path an unclassifiable failure maps to `SYNC_FAILED`, not
  `PROBE_FAILED`: there we do know the sync failed, only not why. An existing
  test caught this over-reach when I first replaced the fallback wholesale.

RA2 — the progress tool and its schema disagreed, and the top level lied.
A run dying before `startIngestionProgress()` still records a synthetic failed
ledger, so the outcome was always reachable — it just was not reported where a
caller reads. The top level said `status: 'idle', errorCount: 0` while the nested
`lastRunSummary` said `failed` with a real count.

- `resolveIdleProgressStatus` separates `never-attempted` / `failed` / `idle`,
  and top-level `errorCount` carries the last run's count rather than a pinned
  zero — a zero beside a failed run is the same false reassurance.
- `observedScope` + `crossProcessHint` now ride EVERY response state, not only
  the idle branch. A partial disclosure is read as a complete one.
- `IngestionProgressResponse` declares `never-attempted` and both scope fields.
  A wire contract omitting what the producer sends is not laxer, it is wrong.
- The scope caveat also went into `x-neo-tool-summary` (79 chars). `description`
  is handbook-only; an agent deciding whether to trust a negative answer sees
  the summary in `tools/list` and nothing else.

The PR body's "all six criteria delivered" was an overshoot and is corrected.

Evidence: 335 green across the twelve specs reading the changed surfaces. New
coverage asserts the four causes resolve to four DISTINCT codes (not four
assertions that would pass against a constant), that a token-bearing fixture
leaks nothing through any of them, and that a non-code cause is refused by the
read boundary. Two existing tests changed expectations because the old coarse
answers were pinned: a fixture whose stderr says "Authentication failed" now
classifies as `CREDENTIAL_REJECTED` instead of `DENIED_OR_NOT_FOUND`, and the
exhaustive persisted-shape assertion declares `lastAccessCode`."
